design_detail: Secondary analysis of a randomized laboratory trial (Howland et al., 2010, designed for simulated driving) comparing two of its parallel groups: young adults who drank beer with added caffeine (n = 28) or the same beer without caffeine (n = 36) to the same breath alcohol target, then had a supervised sleep opportunity at a clinical research centre (conditions in the exposure field); next-morning hangover (Acute Hangover Scale), self-reported sleep and sleepiness. The trial's placebo-beer groups were not analysed. Author manuscript version in PubMed Central.
can_establish: Whether adding a fixed amount of caffeine to beer, at a controlled level of intoxication and with a full night in bed, changed next-morning hangover or self-reported sleep by a large amount in healthy young adults.
cannot_establish: Whether caffeine changes hangover by a small or moderate amount (the interval for hangover incidence runs from 32 percentage points lower to 15 higher; editors' calculation); effects with energy drinks (other ingredients, other amounts), with heavier or later drinking, or with the shortened sleep typical of real nights out; or objective sleep (sleep was self-reported only).

sample.recruitment: Greater Boston, USA; 89% university students, the rest recent graduates; paid 150 US dollars.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 21 to 30; no current or past drinking problems; at least one recent heavy-drinking occasion (definition in the exposure field); no health problems or medication contraindicated with alcohol, no sleep disorder, not pregnant or nursing; regular tobacco use excluded. A prescribed sleep schedule for three nights before the session (diary and time-stamped phone check); abstinence from alcohol, unapproved medication, sleep aids, recreational drugs and caffeine before the session (intervals in the exposure field).
sample.demographics: Caffeinated group: mean age 22.8 (SD 2.3), 41.4% men, 78.6% white, 96% at university; non-caffeinated group: 23.3 (2.1), 58.3% men, 83.3% white, 83% at university; all differences p > 0.20 (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Only completers are reported (28 and 36); how many were randomized to each group is not stated here (it is in the parent trial report, not read). The 41.4% men in a group of 28 is not a possible proportion (12 of 29 gives 41.4%).
sample.selection_effects: Young, healthy, mostly white students without drinking problems, non-smokers, with regulated sleep before the session; volunteers paid to take part.

exposure.measurement: Laboratory-administered drinks, with breath alcohol measured; caffeine added by the investigators as a tasteless solution.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: high-gravity beer (8.1% alcohol by volume) dosed to a breath alcohol of 0.12 g% (1.068 g/kg for men, 0.915 g/kg for women), on average 44 oz of beer (37 oz for women), drunk from 7:30 to about 8:30 p.m. three hours after a standard meal; caffeine added at the concentration of a commercial caffeinated beer (69 mg per 12 oz), on average 383 mg (338 mg for women). Mean peak breath alcohol 0.12 g% (range 0.08 to 0.16) in both groups. Sleep opportunity 11 p.m. to 7 a.m., monitored by an emergency medical technician; Stanford Sleepiness Scale at 8:00, 8:30 and 9:00 a.m. Inclusion required at least one occasion of 5 or more drinks (4 for women) in the previous 30 days; before the session, no alcohol, unapproved medication, sleep aids or recreational drugs for 24 hours and no caffeine for 8 hours.
exposure.polysubstance: Recreational drugs, sleep aids and unapproved medication excluded for 24 hours before the session; regular smokers excluded.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; morning measures after the sleep opportunity (breath alcohol in the morning not reported here).

comparison.controls: A parallel randomized group drinking the same beer without caffeine to the same breath alcohol target.
comparison.matching: Randomized; the method of randomization and any blinding to caffeine are not described in this paper (it refers to the parent trial).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Groups were similar on age, alcohol daily volume, race and university enrolment; men were 41% of the caffeinated and 58% of the non-caffeinated group (not significant). Habitual caffeine use is not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded before the session by instruction.

outcomes.instruments: Acute Hangover Scale (nine items; incidence defined as any rating above none on the first item, severity as the mean of the nine items); six items from a post-sleep questionnaire (Roehrs et al., 1991) giving an average sleep quality score, later split into two night-time and two morning alertness and concentration items; self-reported minutes to fall asleep and minutes asleep; Stanford Sleepiness Scale three times in the morning, averaged.
outcomes.validity_norms: The Acute Hangover Scale is described as psychometrically validated (Rohsenow et al., 2007, by the same group); the sleep-quality items had previously separated heavy drinking from placebo.
outcomes.operationalization: Between-group differences in means (t tests) and proportions (chi-square), with Cohen's d and h, used to judge whether non-significant results reflected small effects or low power.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Outcomes were self-reported by participants; whether they knew they had caffeine is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Caffeinated against non-caffeinated, means (SD): Acute Hangover Scale 1.34 (0.84) against 1.45 (0.89), d = 0.13 (editors' 95% CI for d −0.63 to 0.38); hangover incidence 60.7% against 69.4%, h = 0.19 (editors' risk difference −8.7 percentage points, 95% CI −32 to 15); average sleep quality 4.45 (0.41) against 4.16 (0.49), t(62) = 2.49, 95% CI of the difference 0.057 to 0.517, d = 0.64, better with caffeine; morning alertness and concentration items 4.66 (0.82) against 4.29 (0.93), d = 0.42, p < 0.10; night-time items d = 0.30; minutes to fall asleep 36.5 (67.7) against 23.2 (29.4), d = 0.28; minutes asleep 390.7 (73.8) against 404.7 (62.5), d = 0.21; Stanford Sleepiness 2.52 (1.37) against 2.78 (0.90), d = 0.23; none of these significant except sleep quality.
analysis.covariates: None; the authors argue that dosing by sex and weight and the narrow age range made adjustment unnecessary.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; this is a secondary analysis proposed after the parent trial by a co-author.
analysis.selective_reporting: The split of the sleep-quality score into night-time and morning items was decided after the main result (the Discussion calls it post hoc). The Highlights state that caffeine did not affect next-day mood, but no mood outcome is reported in the paper.
analysis.power: No calculation; the authors use effect sizes to argue that the null results reflect small effects, which the intervals (editors' calculation) do not fully support.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 64 young adults randomized to beer with or without added caffeine at the same breath alcohol, next-morning hangover severity and incidence did not differ detectably (61% against 69% with any hangover), but the intervals are wide enough to include a moderate effect either way. Caffeine did not detectably change self-reported time to fall asleep, time asleep or sleepiness, and the caffeine group rated its sleep quality better, mostly because of morning alertness items.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say mixing caffeine and alcohol does not significantly impair sleep, hangover or sleepiness in this population, which is fair; but the Discussion goes further, saying people who believe adding caffeine to alcohol affects the odds of hangover are likely misinformed and that the results probably generalize to energy drinks and heavier drinking. Gaps: (1) a non-significant difference in 64 people with an interval from 32 points lower to 15 higher cannot show absence of effect; (2) energy drinks, larger amounts and the short sleep of real nights out were not tested; (3) the Highlights report an effect on mood that was not measured in the paper.

timeline.event: Parent randomized trial of caffeinated and non-caffeinated beer on simulated driving (Howland et al., 2010), not read here.
Penning et al. survey of 1503 Dutch students: no difference in hangover severity after drinking with or without energy drinks (as described in this paper).
This secondary analysis: by the authors' account the first randomized comparison of hangover after caffeinated and non-caffeinated alcohol.

replication.where_it_stands: The only randomized test of caffeine added to alcohol on hangover that the authors knew of; its null result agrees in direction with an earlier student survey but is imprecise.

funding.funder: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (grant 1R49CE000946); National Center for Research Resources, NIH (M01 RR00533); a Senior Research Career Scientist Award from the US Department of Veterans Affairs.
funding.declared_conflicts: Howland was principal investigator on a contract between Boston Medical Center and Red Bull GmbH for a student survey on alcohol mixed with energy drinks, stated to be unrelated to this paper. No other conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: The Acute Hangover Scale and the sleep-quality validation cited were developed by the same group (Rohsenow et al., 2006 and 2007).

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized, double-blind trial (with participants' guesses about caffeine recorded) comparing alcohol with and without caffeine or a commercial energy drink, at more than one amount of alcohol and caffeine, with realistic bedtimes, polysomnography or actigraphy, and a prespecified hangover outcome powered to detect a small-to-moderate difference.

domains.note: Described only as randomized, with details deferred to the parent trial; unequal group sizes (28 and 36) and an imbalance in sex (41% against 58% men) without explanation.
Drinks were given and finished under supervision to a breath alcohol target, with a monitored night in the laboratory.
Only completers are reported, with no number randomized; the 41.4% men implies a group of 29 at some stage.
Hangover and sleep were self-reported; whether participants could tell they had caffeine is not reported.
A secondary analysis of a trial designed for driving outcomes, without registration of these outcomes; the sleep-quality score was split after the fact.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The administration of drinks and the night in the laboratory were well controlled, but randomization, blinding and attrition are not reported in this paper, and the outcomes are a later secondary analysis. For the hangover outcome, which is null, the main limitation is imprecision rather than bias. The card may be cited for no detectable difference in next-morning hangover or self-reported sleep after caffeinated against non-caffeinated beer at this level of intoxication, and not for showing that caffeine has no effect on hangover.

key_findings.finding: Hangover did not differ detectably: Acute Hangover Scale 1.34 (SD 0.84) with caffeine against 1.45 (0.89) without, d = 0.13; any hangover 60.7% against 69.4%, h = 0.19.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Acute Hangover Scale and Hangover incidence rows; Results › Hangover, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: d 95% CI −0.63 to 0.38; risk difference −8.7 percentage points (95% CI −32 to 15).

key_findings.finding: The caffeine group reported better average sleep quality (4.45, SD 0.41, against 4.16, SD 0.49; t(62) = 2.49, 95% CI of the difference 0.057 to 0.517; d = 0.64); split afterwards, the morning alertness and concentration items differed more (d = 0.42, p < 0.10) than the night-time items (d = 0.30).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.5 Subjective Sleep Quality and Morning Sleepiness, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Self-reported minutes to fall asleep (36.5 against 23.2), minutes asleep (390.7 against 404.7) and Stanford Sleepiness (2.52 against 2.78) did not differ significantly, with small effect sizes (0.28, 0.21, 0.23).
Peak breath alcohol was the same in both groups, and the caffeine group received caffeine at the concentration of a commercial caffeinated beer (amounts in the exposure field).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.4 Participant characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Methods › 2.3; Table 1

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the null results could reflect low power but argue that the small effect sizes would need very large samples; they suggest the results may differ with older people, other amounts of alcohol or caffeine.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 41.4% men in the caffeinated group of 28; no whole number of 28 gives 41.4% (12 of 29 does; editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Suggests a different denominator at some stage (possibly one more person randomized than analysed); the number randomized is not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Highlights state that caffeine did not affect next-day mood, but no mood measure appears in the Methods or Results.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not a finding of this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give the caffeine content per bottle in millilitres, the abstract the same number in milligrams.
Section numbering is broken: Methods jump from 2.3 to 2.5, and the Results are numbered 2.4 and 2.5, duplicating the Methods' 2.5.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods and Results headings
reporting_issues.consequence: Locators use the printed headings; no effect on content (author manuscript version).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that people who believe caffeine affects the odds of hangover are likely misinformed, from a non-significant difference whose interval includes a moderate effect either way.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say no detectable difference, not no effect.
